contribution: The third unit of the French chapter: beginners order drinks and food in a café, ask what there is, what is in a dish and what it costs, ask for the bill, pay and thank, using the prices from the numbers unit; the café role-play moves from a supported three-step dialogue and an authentic teacher-made video to free pair speaking with secret role cards.
learn: order drinks and food politely in a French café.
ask what there is, what is in a dish and what it costs, and understand the waiter's answers.
pay, thank and hold a whole café conversation in a role-play without a script.
prior: Greetings, *tu* and *vous* (chapter *Bonjour ! Introducing yourself*)

activities.text: It is half past one. After a morning at the ITER site, you and a friend sit down at a café terrace in the shade of the plane trees. The menu is on the table, everything is in French, and the waiter is coming towards you with a tray. You are hungry, you have about ten euros each, and you want to pay before the bus leaves at half past two.
activities.question: What will you need to say during the next hour, and in which order?

activities.text:
Sentence starters

  • First we need to …, then …
  • In a Finnish café you usually …, but …
  • I already know the French words …
  • The hardest part could be …, because …

activities.title: Think about it: a café visit step by step
activities.prompt: List the steps of a café visit, from the moment you sit down to the moment you leave. How does it go in a Finnish café: do you order at the counter or at the table? Then write every French café word you already know (drinks, food, phrases).
activities.pair: Discuss with a partner for three minutes, then write your list together.
activities.model: Steps: sit down and read the menu, greet the waiter, order drinks and food, ask about anything we do not understand, eat, thank and say goodbye. In many Finnish cafés we order at the counter and carry our own tray; at a French café terrace the waiter usually takes the order at the table. French words we know: café, croissant, crêpe, baguette, croque-monsieur, bon appétit, merci, s'il vous plaît.
criteria: We list the steps in a sensible order: greet, order, ask, eat, thank.
We compare at least one step with a Finnish café.
We list some French café words.

activities.title: Prediction 1: the first words
activities.prompt: The waiter comes to your table and says « Bonjour ! Vous avez choisi ? » Which answer is the most polite and natural? Commit now; the theory summary will show you.

choices.text: Bonjour. Un café, s'il vous plaît.
choices.feedback: Right: a greeting, a short order and s'il vous plaît. Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît is just as good. In France the greeting comes first, every time.
Je veux (I want) is correct French, but to a waiter it sounds like a demand, and there is no greeting. Say Bonjour. Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.

choices.text: Garçon ! Un café, s'il vous plaît.
choices.feedback: Garçon (boy) was once the usual way to call a waiter; today many people find it old-fashioned or rude. Answer his greeting: Bonjour. Un café, s'il vous plaît.

choices.text: Salut ! Tu me donnes un café ?
choices.feedback: Salut and tu are for friends and people your age. The waiter is an adult you do not know: Bonjour. Un café, s'il vous plaît.

activities.title: Prediction 2: the bill
activities.prompt: You finished eating ten minutes ago, and the waiter has not brought the bill. Your bus leaves soon. What is the best thing to do? Commit now; the theory summary will show you.

choices.feedback: Right. The waiter usually does not hurry you, and the bill often comes only when you ask for it: L'addition, s'il vous plaît.

choices.text: Wait: the waiter will bring it soon.
choices.feedback: Perhaps, but the waiter usually does not hurry you, and the bill often comes only when you ask for it: L'addition, s'il vous plaît. If you only wait, you may miss your bus.

choices.text: Go to the kitchen to find the waiter.
choices.feedback: Customers do not go into the kitchen. Catch the waiter's eye from your table, or say Excusez-moi ! when he passes, and ask: L'addition, s'il vous plaît.

choices.text: Leave the money on the table and go.
choices.feedback: You do not know the total yet, and the waiter may not see you leave. Ask for the bill first: L'addition, s'il vous plaît.

activities.title: Listen: the phrases of a café visit
activities.text: Listen to each phrase, first slowly and then at normal speed, and repeat it aloud. The hints in italics use Finnish letters: capitals show the stressed syllable, and *õ*, *ã* and *ẽ* are nasal vowels; *č* is the *ch* of English *church*.

activities.title: A lunch at the café
activities.text: Read the dialogue and notice three things: the order of the steps, the phrase the customer uses to order, and how she gets the bill.

activities.title: Watch: another café dialogue
activities.text: Now watch a short café dialogue made by a French teacher. Watch once with the English subtitles. Watch again and note: (1) how the customer greets, (2) what is ordered, (3) any question or price you hear, (4) how the visit ends. Then find one phrase in the video that is different from the dialogue above, and the spelling mistake the author warns about.

activities.title: Order a café conversation
What did you notice?
activities.prompt: In the conversation you put in order, Eetu and Léa say *vous* to the waiter but *tu* to each other. Why?

choices.text: They don't know the waiter; they are friends.
choices.feedback: Yes. The choice depends on the person: vous with an adult you do not know, such as a waiter, and tu between friends of the same age.

choices.text: *Vous* is only used for ordering food and drinks.
choices.feedback: Vous is not tied to ordering. It is the polite form for an adult you do not know, and the form for more than one person. Between friends, tu.

choices.text: Because the waiter is older than sixty.
choices.feedback: His age is not given, and age alone does not decide it. A waiter is someone you do not know, in a work situation, so you use vous.

choices.text: Because Léa is French and Eetu is Finnish.
choices.feedback: Where they come from does not matter. Friends of the same age say tu to each other, and both say vous to the waiter.

sections: At a French café: what happens when

activities.title: Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your two predictions with the theory. Then answer the opening question in English in one or two sentences: why can about ten short phrases get you through a whole café visit in France? Name the step where each of your predictions belongs.

activities.title: Complete the order
Understand the waiter
Role-play: from script to free speaking
activities.text:
Work in pairs, with the menu above. Each round gives you less support. **Round 1 (cues):** perform the dialogue *A lunch at the café* again in step 3 (*Perform*), from the English cues only. Change the drink and the dish, and the total with them. **Rounds 2 and 3 (role cards):** one partner is the customer, the other the waiter. Open only your own card below (*Customer only* or *Waiter only*), do not show it, and speak without writing first. The other partner has information that you do not have, so listen and react. Swap the roles in round 3.

Word bank

Bonjour, madame / monsieur, Vous avez choisi ?, Je voudrais …, Je vais prendre …, Et avec ça ?, Qu'est-ce que vous avez comme … ?, Qu'est-ce qu'il y a dans … ?, C'est combien, … ?, L'addition, s'il vous plaît, Ça fait …, par carte, en espèces, Gardez la monnaie, Merci, bonne journée

Sentence starters

  • Bonjour, monsieur. Je voudrais …, s'il vous plaît.
  • C'est combien, la tarte ?
  • Excusez-moi ! L'addition, s'il vous plaît.
  • Je peux payer par carte ?
  • Merci beaucoup. Au revoir !

The waiter: Ça fait … euros …, Bon appétit !, Je vous apporte ça tout de suite.

activities.title: Round 2: customer card
activities.text: You are hungry, but you do not eat meat. You have 10 € and want a hot drink too. Ask what is in at least one dish and ask one price before you order. Pay by card. Useful: Qu'est-ce qu'il y a dans le croque-monsieur ? Ah, je ne mange pas de viande. Alors, je vais prendre …

activities.title: Round 2: waiter card
activities.text: Today there are no more croissants: Désolé, il n'y a plus de croissants. The quiche has vegetables and cheese; the croque-monsieur has ham and cheese. Answer the customer's questions, give the total and take the card.

activities.title: Round 3: customer card
activities.text: You order for two: you and your friend (your partner's imaginary friend). Order two different drinks and one dessert to share. Ask the price of one dessert. Pay in cash and let the waiter keep the change.

activities.title: Round 3: waiter card
activities.text: The card reader does not work today: cash only (Désolé, seulement en espèces.). Recommend a dessert (Je vous conseille la tarte aux pommes.). Give the total and thank the customers.

activities.title: Role-play: your dialogue
activities.prompt: After round 2, write down in French the dialogue you performed, at least eight lines. Mark the line where you reacted to something you did not know in advance.
activities.pair: Perform round 2 with your partner first, then write it together. If you can, perform it for another pair, who check it with the criteria below.
activities.model: - Serveur : Bonjour ! Vous avez choisi ? - Cliente : Bonjour, monsieur. Je voudrais un chocolat chaud, s'il vous plaît. - Serveur : Très bien. Et avec ça ? - Cliente : Un croissant, s'il vous plaît. - Serveur : Désolé, il n'y a plus de croissants. - Cliente : Ah ! Qu'est-ce qu'il y a dans la quiche ? - Serveur : Des légumes et du fromage. - Cliente : C'est combien, la quiche ? - Serveur : Huit euros quatre-vingt-dix. - Cliente : Hmm, je vais prendre la tarte aux pommes, alors. - Cliente : … L'addition, s'il vous plaît. - Serveur : Un chocolat chaud et une tarte : ça fait huit euros trente. - Cliente : Je peux payer par carte ? - Serveur : Oui, bien sûr. Voilà. - Cliente : Merci beaucoup. Bonne journée ! The reaction: there are no more croissants, so the customer asks about the quiche, finds it too expensive with the drink (3,80 € + 8,90 € = 12,70 €, over the 10 € budget) and takes the tart (3,80 € + 4,50 € = 8,30 €).
criteria: **Communicates the message:** we greet, order a drink and food, ask at least one question about a dish or a price, ask for the bill, pay and thank.
**Polite:** the customer uses *vous*, *je voudrais* or *je vais prendre* and *s'il vous plaît*.
**Reacts:** we answer something we did not know in advance (a missing dish, cash only) instead of reading a script.
**Numbers right:** the prices and the total match the menu.

activities.title: Extension: ordering coffee in real life
activities.text: This video is from a channel that films everyday French. Watch it with subtitles. Note every coffee word you hear (for example *un café*, *un crème*, *un allongé*, *une noisette*) and two phrases for ordering that are not in this lesson. Tell your partner which one you will use next time.

activities.title: 1. Asking a price
activities.prompt: You want to know what the vegetable quiche costs. What do you ask the waiter?

choices.feedback: Yes. C'est combien … ? asks the price of one thing.

choices.text: Il y a combien de quiches ?
choices.feedback: This asks *how many quiches are there?*, a number, not a price. Ask C'est combien, la quiche ?
This asks whether they have a quiche, not what it costs: C'est combien, la quiche ?
This asks whether the quiche is good. For the price: C'est combien, la quiche ?

activities.title: 2. Friends and the waiter
activities.prompt: You are at the café with a French friend of your age. You want to ask *her* what she is having. What do you say?

choices.feedback: Yes. She is a friend of your age, so you use tu. To the waiter you would say vous.
This is what the waiter says to customers, with vous. To a friend of your age: Tu prends quoi ?
This is your own order, not a question to her: Tu prends quoi ?
This asks a price. To ask your friend what she is having: Tu prends quoi ?

activities.title: 3. Paying
activities.prompt: The bill is 9,40 €. You give the waiter a 10 € note and want him to keep the 60 centimes. What do you say?

choices.feedback: You already have the bill: this phrase asks for it. To let him keep the rest: Gardez la monnaie.
Yes: *keep the change*. A tip is not required in France, because the service is included, but rounding up is common.
This asks for your change, the opposite of what you want. Say Gardez la monnaie.
This is what the waiter says when he gives a total. To let him keep the change: Gardez la monnaie.

activities.title: 4. Write: your order
activities.prompt: Write a short café conversation (six to eight lines) for you and a friend: greet the waiter, order two drinks and one thing to eat from the menu, ask one question, ask for the bill and pay. Use *vous* with the waiter and *tu* with your friend.
activities.model: - Serveuse : Bonjour ! Vous désirez ? - Moi : Bonjour, madame. Je voudrais une limonade, s'il vous plaît. Eetu, tu prends quoi ? - Eetu : Un thé, s'il vous plaît. - Moi : Qu'est-ce qu'il y a dans le croque-monsieur ? - Serveuse : Du jambon et du fromage. - Moi : Alors un croque-monsieur, s'il vous plaît. … L'addition, s'il vous plaît. - Serveuse : Ça fait quatorze euros. - Moi : Voilà. Merci, au revoir ! (3,50 € + 3,00 € + 7,50 € = 14,00 €)
criteria: I greet and order with *je voudrais* or *je vais prendre* and *s'il vous plaît*.
I ask one question about a dish or a price and ask for *l'addition*.
I use *vous* with the waiter and *tu* with my friend.
